youtube.baslik: Bone-Conduction Implants: Percutaneous vs Transcutaneous | Lesson 249 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How do we get sound to the cochlea when there is no ear canal, or the ear drains constantly? In this lesson we cover candidacy for bone-conduction implants, percutaneous and active and passive transcutaneous systems, softband trials, choosing device power from bone-conduction thresholds, in situ measurement and use in single-sided deafness.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tjellström, Håkansson and Granström (2001), Bone-anchored hearing aids: current status in adults and children, Otolaryngologic Clinics of North America; Holgers et al. (1988), Soft tissue reactions around percutaneous implants, American Journal of Otology; Reinfeldt et al. (2015), New developments in bone-conduction hearing implants: a review, Medical Devices: Evidence and Research; Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about bone-conduction implants, which send sound directly to the cochlea through skull vibration.
We will cover candidacy, systems that pass through the skin and systems under it, trials on a band, and choosing device power.
In the bone conduction lesson, we saw that when the skull vibrates, sound reaches the cochlea largely bypassing the outer and middle ear.
Bone-conduction implants use this principle: sound does not have to pass through the ear canal and the middle ear.
The device turns the sound it picks up into vibration and passes this vibration to the temporal bone.
The vibration spreads through the skull and moves the cochlear fluids, creating the sensation of hearing.
So as long as the cochlea works well, sound can reach it, however severe the problem in the outer or middle ear.
For success, bone-conduction thresholds, that is, cochlear sensitivity, must lie within the range the device's power can cover.
Atresia, where the ear canal never developed, and microtia, where the pinna is underdeveloped, are classic indications.
In chronic middle ear disease with constant or frequent drainage, a device that blocks the ear canal can make drainage worse.
In these ears, the ear canal stays open and sound is delivered by bone conduction.
People who cannot use a hearing aid because of canal allergy or a narrow or surgically altered ear canal are also candidates.
In conductive or mixed losses, these systems work well when bone-conduction thresholds are within the device's range.
In single-sided deafness, the device carries sound from the deaf side by bone conduction to the healthy cochlea on the other side.
Candidacy is decided by the team, based on audiological findings, the medical state of the ear and the person's preference.
In this example, the right ear has congenital atresia; air-conduction thresholds lie between sixty and seventy decibels.
Masked bone-conduction thresholds, however, are within normal limits; in other words, the cochlea works well.
There is an air-bone gap of about fifty decibels; this is close to the largest conductive loss expected in atresia.
Without an ear canal, an air-conduction aid cannot be worn; but normal bone conduction shows a bone-conduction device can work very well.
The values are only an example; the actual decision is made together with imaging and the ear surgeon's evaluation.
Nonsurgical forms of bone-conduction devices are worn on a headband or on an adhesive pad stuck to the skin.
In percutaneous systems, which pass through the skin, a part attached to an implant in the bone comes out through the skin.
The sound processor attaches directly to this part and passes vibration directly to the bone.
In transcutaneous systems, which stay under the skin, the skin remains intact.
In passive transcutaneous systems, the processor holds onto a magnet under the skin, and vibration passes through the skin to the bone.
In active transcutaneous systems, the vibrating part sits under the skin on the bone; the external processor sends it power and signal.
Each approach has different advantages for sound transmission, skin problems, appearance and care.

cumleler.yazi: The first bone-anchored hearing aid was fitted in 1977 in Gothenburg, Sweden, by Tjellström and colleagues.
cumleler.ses: The first bone-anchored hearing aid was fitted in nineteen seventy seven in Gothenburg, Sweden, by Tjellström and colleagues.

cumleler: A small titanium screw is placed in the temporal bone behind the ear.
Over time, the titanium fuses directly with the bone; this is called osseointegration, and only then is the processor attached.
The abutment, the connecting part attached to the screw, comes out through the skin, and the sound processor clips onto it.
Because vibration goes straight to the bone without passing through skin and soft tissue, this is one of the most efficient systems.
These systems are generally called bone-anchored hearing systems.
In the US, these implants are limited to children aged five and older; younger children use the device on a band.
Skin reactions such as redness, discharge or tissue overgrowth may be seen around the abutment that passes through the skin.
These reactions are recorded with the Holgers classification, which grades them from zero to four.
Grade zero means no reaction, and grade four a severe reaction that may require removal of the implant.
Most reactions are mild and settle with local care; but treatment decisions belong to the physician.
More rarely, the fusion of titanium with bone fails, and the implant may loosen and be lost.
The person is taught to clean around the abutment gently every day and to report any skin changes.
In a passive transcutaneous system, a magnet under the skin holds the processor in place; with intact skin, skin care problems are few.
However, as vibration passes through skin and soft tissue, it can lose up to about ten to twenty decibels, especially at high frequencies.
Also, magnet pressure can cause skin pain or redness with long use; so magnet strength is chosen carefully.
In an active transcutaneous system, the transducer that creates vibration is placed under the skin, directly on the bone.
The external processor picks up sound and sends power and signal through the skin to the internal part, much like a cochlear implant.
Because vibration is created under the skin, there is no skin loss; but these systems require more extensive surgery.
For all systems that contain a magnet, magnetic resonance imaging is planned according to the manufacturer's conditions.
In this schematic graph, the navy line represents vibration passed directly to the bone.
The blue line shows the same vibration passed through skin and soft tissue.
Skin weakens vibration, especially at high frequencies; the difference grows as frequency rises.
This loss appears both in passive transcutaneous systems and in trials where the device is worn on a band.
So a trial on a band often makes the sound after implantation seem a little worse than it will really be.
The values vary with the person and skin thickness; the graph shows only the trend.
Evaluation starts with reliable bone-conduction thresholds, obtained for each ear separately and with masking when needed.
Next, the sound processor is tried on the head with a softband or an adhesive pad.
The person uses the device for a few days or weeks in their own daily settings and forms concrete expectations.
Aided sound field thresholds and speech tests can also be done during the trial.
Based on bone-conduction thresholds, a standard, power or super power model of the device is chosen.
The final decision is made by the team, together with trial results, the medical state of the ear and the person's preference.
In children younger than five, the softband is often not just a trial but a long-term way of wearing the device.
Device power is chosen from the average bone-conduction threshold, usually the average at five hundred, one, two and three thousand hertz.
Standard-power percutaneous devices are recommended for people with a bone-conduction average of about forty five decibels HL or better.
Stronger models fit bone-conduction thresholds up to about fifty five, the strongest up to about sixty five decibels HL, by manufacturer.
These limits vary by manufacturer, model and type of system; transcutaneous systems may have different ranges.
In single-sided deafness, air-conduction thresholds in the better ear of about twenty decibels HL or better are required.
If bone-conduction thresholds are near the limit, the option of moving to a stronger model if the loss progresses is also discussed.
In single-sided deafness, the bone-conduction device is placed on the deaf side and picks up sound from that side.
The vibration travels across the skull to the healthy cochlea on the other side.
So speech from the deaf side reaches the good ear without being blocked by the head shadow.
Although interaural attenuation for bone conduction is taken as zero in the clinic, it can reach fifteen decibels at high frequencies.
As with contralateral routing of signals, or CROS, all sounds reach a single cochlea here; localization does not return.
As we saw in the previous lessons, the choice among options in single-sided deafness is made after all paths are explained without bias.
Thresholds measured with a bone vibrator on the audiometer do not exactly reflect the vibration the processor delivers to the person's head.
Skull structure, skin thickness and how the device is attached change transmission from person to person.
So during fitting, thresholds are measured using the sound processor itself as the vibration source; this is called in situ measurement.
The fitting software calculates gain from these in situ thresholds, so the real vibration reaching the person is taken into account.
Real ear measurement in the ear canal is not possible with bone-conduction devices; output can instead be measured with a skull simulator.
The result is verified with aided sound field thresholds and speech in noise tests.
For reimbursement of bone-conduction implants in Türkiye, the current Health Implementation Communiqué should always be checked.

sahneler.metin: In a band trial, explain that skin loss makes the sound weaker than after implantation. Run the trial in the person's own daily settings.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: during a band trial, tell the person that after implantation the sound will usually be a little stronger and clearer.
This is because on a band the vibration passes through the skin and weakens, especially at high frequencies.
Have the trial done not only in a quiet clinic room, but at the person's home, work and school.
In single-sided deafness, note together at the end of the trial in which settings the person found benefit.

maddeler.metin: Sound reaches the cochlea through bone

cumleler: Bone-conduction implants bypass the outer and middle ear and deliver sound to the cochlea through skull vibration.
Percutaneous systems pass vibration directly to the bone and are efficient; the abutment through the skin needs regular care.
In passive transcutaneous systems the skin is intact but high frequencies are lost; in active systems the vibrator is under the skin.
Device power is chosen from bone-conduction thresholds, the decision follows a band trial, and fitting uses in situ measurement.

sahneler.soru: What is device power based on?
sahneler.aciklama: The device stimulates the cochlea directly; the key is the _bone-conduction_ thresholds.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which measurement is the basis for choosing the power of a bone-conduction implant?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: bone-conduction thresholds.
The device bypasses the outer and middle ear to stimulate the cochlea, so the power needed depends on bone-conduction thresholds.
